title: The morning blessings
hook: a chain of thanks for waking: sight, clothing, standing upright

segments.voice: Yesterday, mah tovu, Balaam's words said on entering a synagogue. Your line was how good these tents. Which doorway did you pause at? Today, the very first prayers of the morning. Day five hundred forty-two.

Before coffee, before the phone, before anyone has said a word to you, a lot has already gone right. Your eyes opened. You could tell it was morning. You sat up, you found something to wear, and your feet held you when you stood. None of it feels like news. It's the floor the day is built on, and nobody thanks a floor. The Jewish morning service begins by thanking it anyway, one piece at a time: a short chain of blessings, each fitted to something a waking body just did. Today, the chain itself.
screen: `BEFORE COFFEE, A LOT WENT RIGHT.` → `NOBODY THANKS A FLOOR.` → `A CHAIN OF THANKS.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew they're called birchot hashachar, the blessings of the dawn. Each one opens with the same words, baruch atah, blessed are you, and then names one gift. Who opens the eyes of the blind. Who clothes the naked. Who raises up the bowed down. Who makes firm a person's steps. Where did they come from? The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, page sixty b, walks through a person's waking. When you hear the rooster, say this. When you open your eyes, say this. When you sit up, when you dress, when you stand, when your feet touch the ground, when you put on your shoes. A blessing for each motion, said at the moment it happened. So in the Talmud's telling, these blessings belong to the bedroom, not the synagogue. Over the centuries many communities moved them into the service and said them as a list. One explanation: hands weren't yet washed at the bedside, and not everyone knew the words, so the leader said them aloud and everyone answered amen. Maimonides didn't like the change. He held that each blessing belongs to its own moment. Today some people say a few at home as they wake, and many also say them together in the service. Either way, the order still follows a body getting up: hearing, seeing, sitting, dressing, standing, walking. Underneath is a simple rule. The Talmud teaches that a person shouldn't enjoy anything in this world without a blessing, and waking up is the first thing you enjoy. Sight and steady legs aren't treated as small just because they're common. The list is a way of noticing the basics before the day buries them.
screen: `BIRCHOT HASHACHAR: BLESSINGS OF DAWN.` · `A BLESSING FOR EACH MOTION.` · `FROM THE BEDROOM TO THE SERVICE.` · `NO JOY WITHOUT A BLESSING.` · then, large: `THANKS FOR THE BASICS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for three things your body does. Settle, and breathe. Start with the breath itself, going in and out without being asked. Then pick two more. Your eyes, taking in the room. Your hands, which have already done a hundred small jobs today. Your heartbeat. Your hearing. For each one, stay a few breaths and simply notice it working. If you pray, you can begin each with the words baruch atah, blessed are you. If you don't, a plain thank you is enough. The bell holds the time.
Birchot hashachar. The blessings of the dawn: a chain of short thanks for waking, seeing, dressing and standing.
Your line: thanks for the basics. Today, when you do one ordinary thing, open a door, tie a shoe, stand up from a chair, give it one second of thanks. Day five hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Many Jews say the morning blessings at the start of the weekday and Shabbat morning service, often led aloud by the prayer leader with the congregation answering amen, and some say them at home on waking.

fork.setup: you lead prayers long ago. many people in the room don't know the morning blessings by heart. what do you do?
options: skip them in public; they belong at home.
say them aloud and let everyone answer amen.

fork.reveal: many communities did just this: the leader said the blessings aloud and the congregation answered amen. it's one reason a bedside practice ended up in the prayer book.

notes: Berakhot 60b: the sequence of waking blessings (rooster, eyes, sitting up, dressing, standing, stepping, shoes, etc.); confirm the order as summarized.

Reasons for moving the blessings into the synagogue (unwashed hands; people who didn't know them; leader recites for all) follow the Tur and later codes; confirm attribution and phrasing 'one explanation'.
Maimonides, Laws of Prayer 7:9: his objection to reciting the blessings in synagogue when not at the moment; confirm citation.
Berakhot 35a: forbidden to benefit from this world without a blessing; paraphrased.
'Who raises up the bowed down' (zokef kefufim) is rendered loosely; confirm English renderings of the blessings.
Review pass: 'these blessings started in the bedroom' softened to 'in the Talmud's telling'; 'most also say them' softened to 'many'. Customs on home vs. synagogue recitation vary by community.
